text: In one novel by this author, a boy tricks his friends into whitewashing a fence in St. Petersburg, Missouri. A sequel narrated by that boy's friend Huckleberry Finn follows a journey down the Mississippi River with the escaped slave Jim. For 10 points, name this American author of "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer," who wrote under a pen name.

This man's first inaugural address declared that "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself." He created programs like the Civilian Conservation Corps and Social Security as part of the New Deal. Elected four times, he led the United States for most of World War II. For 10 points, name this president, nicknamed "FDR."

This organelle contains folds called cristae and an inner space called the matrix. Its own circular DNA is cited as evidence for the endosymbiotic theory. Most of a cell's ATP is produced here through oxidative phosphorylation. For 10 points, name this "powerhouse of the cell."

Allotropes of this element include graphite, diamond, and buckminsterfullerene. Its isotope with mass number 14 is used in radiometric dating. With atomic number 6, it forms four covalent bonds and is the basis of organic chemistry. For 10 points, name this element with chemical symbol C.

This painter's "Irises" and "Café Terrace at Night" were completed in the final years of his life. After an argument with Paul Gauguin in Arles, he cut off part of his own ear. His works include a series of sunflowers and "The Starry Night." For 10 points, name this Dutch Post-Impressionist.

This country's Great Barrier Reef lies off its northeastern coast, and its red center contains the monolith Uluru. Its capital is Canberra, though its largest city is Sydney. Kangaroos and koalas are native to this country. For 10 points, name this island country and continent in the Southern Hemisphere.

This hero was driven mad by Hera and killed his own family, then performed penance for King Eurystheus. His tasks included cleaning the Augean stables, capturing Cerberus, and slaying the Nemean lion. For 10 points, name this Greek hero, the son of Zeus and Alcmene, called Hercules by the Romans.

According to the Book of Exodus, this man was hidden as a baby in a basket among the reeds of the Nile. He confronted a burning bush and called down ten plagues upon Egypt. He later received the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai. For 10 points, name this prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt.

Euclid proved that there are infinitely many examples of this type of number. His argument multiplies any finite list of them together and adds one. A number of this type has exactly two positive divisors, one and itself. For 10 points, name this type of number, examples of which are 2, 3, 5, and 7.

In binary, this number is written as 10, and it is the base of that number system. It is the only even prime number, and the square root of this number is irrational. It is the smallest prime, and a pair of anything has this many members. For 10 points, give this number, the successor of one.

text: The lawyer Mr. Jaggers and the convict Magwitch appear in one novel by this author, which features Pip and the jilted Miss Havisham. Another of his novels features Sydney Carton, who sacrifices himself during the French Revolution, and opens with "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times." For 10 points, name this Victorian author of "Oliver Twist" and "A Tale of Two Cities."

This man took power in the coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 and promulgated a civil code that bears his name. He crowned himself emperor at Notre-Dame in 1804 and was defeated at the Battle of Leipzig and, after returning from Elba, at Waterloo. He died in exile on Saint Helena. For 10 points, name this French emperor.

Johann Loschmidt estimated a related constant for the number of molecules per volume of gas. This quantity is named for an Italian scientist who proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles. For 10 points, name this number, approximately 6.022 times ten to the twenty-third, the number of particles in one mole.

Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51 provided crucial X-ray diffraction evidence for the structure of this molecule. Erwin Chargaff showed that its adenine and thymine, and its guanine and cytosine, occur in equal amounts. James Watson and Francis Crick described its double helix in 1953. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that stores genetic information.

This composer wrote six concertos dedicated to the Margrave of Brandenburg and a set of preludes and fugues titled "The Well-Tempered Clavier." He served as Kantor of the Thomaskirche in Leipzig and wrote the Mass in B minor and the Goldberg Variations. For 10 points, name this Baroque German composer of the "Toccata and Fugue in D minor."

The Aswan High Dam on this river created Lake Nasser. Its two main tributaries are the White and Blue branches, which meet at Khartoum. It flows north through Sudan and Egypt and empties into the Mediterranean through a large delta. For 10 points, name this longest river of Africa, whose valley hosted ancient Egyptian civilization.

This man was born in Lumbini as a prince, and left his palace after seeing an old man, a sick man, and a corpse. He practiced extreme asceticism before achieving enlightenment under a Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya. His first sermon at Sarnath set out the Four Noble Truths. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

This thinker wrote that an evil demon might deceive him about everything, and he doubted all he could in order to find a foundation for knowledge. His "Meditations on First Philosophy" and "Discourse on Method" argue for mind-body dualism. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who wrote "I think, therefore I am."

This economist described a division of labor in a pin factory, using it to explain how specialization improves productivity. He argued that individuals pursuing their own interest are led as if by an "invisible hand" to benefit society. For 10 points, name this Scottish economist who wrote "The Wealth of Nations" in 1776.

This scientist explained the photoelectric effect by proposing that light comes in quanta, work for which he won the 1921 Nobel Prize. He explained Brownian motion in his annus mirabilis of 1905, the year he published his special theory of relativity. His general theory of relativity describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime. For 10 points, name this physicist who wrote "E equals m c squared."

text: This author's epic includes a character who tells of Francesca da Rimini and Paolo being blown about by a whirlwind, and another who describes Count Ugolino gnawing on a skull. In it, the Roman poet Virgil guides the narrator through nine circles, while Beatrice leads him through Paradise. For 10 points, name this Florentine author of the "Divine Comedy."

In this author's best-known novel, the patriarch José Arcadio Buendía founds the village of Macondo, and a plague of insomnia strikes the town. The story ends when the last Buendía deciphers Melquíades's parchments. A pioneer of magical realism, he won the 1982 Nobel Prize. For 10 points, name this Colombian author of "One Hundred Years of Solitude."

A traitor named Ephialtes revealed a mountain path that let the Persians outflank the defenders in this battle. King Leonidas stayed behind with 300 Spartans and a force of Thespians and Thebans. Xerxes's invasion forces overwhelmed the defenders at this 480 BC pass in Greece. For 10 points, name this battle, a famous last stand.

The Judiciary Act of 1789 and William Marbury's undelivered commission as a justice of the peace were at issue in this case. In it, Chief Justice John Marshall wrote that a law contrary to the Constitution is void. For 10 points, name this 1803 Supreme Court case that established judicial review.

Ludwig Boltzmann's tombstone is inscribed with an equation defining this quantity as a constant times the logarithm of the number of microstates. Rudolf Clausius coined its name. The second law of thermodynamics states that this quantity in an isolated system never decreases. For 10 points, name this measure of disorder, symbolized S.

This mathematician scribbled a note in the margin of a copy of Diophantus's "Arithmetica" claiming a marvelous proof that was too large for the margin. His little theorem states that a to the p, minus a, is divisible by prime p. For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose "last theorem" was proved by Andrew Wiles in the 1990s.

This architect designed the Casa Batlló and Casa Milà, and the undulating bench of Park Güell. His unfinished masterpiece in Barcelona has towers with Nativity, Passion, and Glory facades. For 10 points, name this Catalan architect of the Sagrada Família.

This god sacrificed an eye at Mímir's well in exchange for wisdom, and he hung for nine nights on Yggdrasil to learn the runes. His ravens Huginn and Muninn gather news for him, and his eight-legged horse is Sleipnir. For 10 points, name this one-eyed leader of the Aesir who is killed by the wolf Fenrir at Ragnarok.

The Serengeti plains and the volcano Kilimanjaro lie in this country, which includes the island of Zanzibar. Its largest city is Dar es Salaam, though its official capital was moved to Dodoma. For 10 points, name this East African country, formed by the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar, whose neighbors include Kenya.

A metronome and later a bell were sounded before food was delivered in experiments by this researcher, who measured the salivation of dogs. His work on classical conditioning revealed that a neutral stimulus can evoke a conditioned response. For 10 points, name this Russian physiologist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
